title: Steganography: hidden data in images
description: LSB in pixels, JPEG COM segments, data past a PNG's IEND: three ways to hide and three to find.

1.title: LSB in BMP and JPEG COM
1.body:
## LSB: the pixel classic

A 24-bit BMP image stores 3 bytes per pixel (RGB). Changing the least
significant bit (LSB) of a channel shifts the color by 1/256 — invisible
to the eye. A 64×64 pixel-art image holds 4096 bits: more than enough for a message.

The lab's scheme: first 32 bits = message length (LE), then the
message, 1 bit per byte of the pixel data:

```bash
curl -O http://127.0.0.1:18105/bmp-lago.bmp
```

```python
# extract_lsb.py — the go-to extractor
import struct
data = open('bmp-lago.bmp','rb').read()
px = data[54:]                       # BMP headers = 14 + 40 bytes
def bits(n):  return [px[i] & 1 for i in range(n)]
def tobytes(bs):
    out = bytearray()
    for i in range(0, len(bs), 8):
        b = 0
        for bit in bs[i:i+8]: b = (b << 1) | bit
        out.append(b)
    return bytes(out)
length = struct.unpack('<I', tobytes(bits(32)))[0]
msg = tobytes(bits(32 + length*8)[32:])
print(msg.decode())
```

In real CTFs `zsteg` (PNG/BMP) and `stegsolve` do this and much more,
but knowing how to write the extractor teaches you what they look for.

## JPEG COM: metadata with substance

JPEG is a segment-based format: `FF E0` APP0, `FF DB` DQT... and `FF FE`
**COM**, a free-form comment that any editor can write. Nobody
sees it when opening the image, but it's there:

```bash
curl -O http://127.0.0.1:18105/vacaciones.jpg
strings vacaciones.jpg | grep -i flag
exiftool vacaciones.jpg       # the pro alternative: Comment: secret: FLAG{...}
```

**Defensive lesson**: DLP tools that only look at extensions miss
metadata; attackers exfiltrate through EXIF/COM fields nobody audits.

steganography-t01-q01.prompt: Download bmp-lago.bmp from the lab. The first 32 pixel LSBs hold the length (little-endian) then the message. Submit the flag.
steganography-t01-q01.hint: python: read the bytes from offset 54, take the least significant bit of each byte, group them 8 at a time (MSB first)

steganography-t01-q02.prompt: Download vacaciones.jpg. The flag lives in a JPEG COM (comment) segment. Submit it.
steganography-t01-q02.hint: strings vacaciones.jpg | grep FLAG — or exiftool vacaciones.jpg

2.title: Data past IEND and double files
2.body:
## The concatenated file trick

A well-formed PNG ends with the `IEND` chunk (CRC included). Decoders
stop there and **ignore everything that comes after it**. That
turns any PNG into an envelope: append a ZIP at the end and the image
looks identical.

```bash
curl -O http://127.0.0.1:18105/logo-corp.png

# Option 1: binwalk detects embedded signatures
binwalk logo-corp.png
# Decimal    Hex        Description
# 0          0x0        PNG image
# N          0xN        Zip archive data

# Option 2: by hand with python
python3 -c "
import zipfile
# zipfile reads the End of Central Directory from the END of the file,
# so it opens the PNG 'with the glued zip' without trimming anything:
z = zipfile.ZipFile('logo-corp.png')
print(z.namelist())
print(z.read('notas-secretas.txt').decode())
"
```

`unzip` swallows it too: `unzip logo-corp.png` (it complains about "extra
data at beginning" but extracts anyway).

## The reverse trick: polyglots

The same idea turned around produces **polyglot files** (valid as two
formats at once): GIFAR (GIF+JAR), PDF+DOC... Antivirus scanners and
upload validators that only read the header swallow them whole. That's why serious
uploads validate the full content, not the extension or just
the first magic bytes.

## The analyst's stego kit

| Tool | What for |
|---|---|
| `strings` / `grep` | First thing, always: text inside binaries |
| `binwalk` | Embedded signatures (zip, ELF, nested PNGs) |
| `exiftool` | EXIF/COM image metadata |
| `zsteg` / `stegsolve` | LSB and bit planes (PNG/BMP) |
| `steghide` | LSB with a passphrase (JPEG/BMP/WAV) |
| `xxd` | When nothing else works: look at the bytes |

steganography-t02-q01.prompt: logo-corp.png is a valid PNG BUT weighs more than it should: a ZIP is glued after IEND. Extract its contents and submit the flag.
steganography-t02-q01.hint: binwalk logo-corp.png → zip at offset N; or python: find IEND and open the rest with zipfile

steganography-t02-q02.prompt: What hexadecimal signature marks the end of a PNG (the chunk after which the file should end)? Write the 4 ASCII characters.
